content: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute condition characterized by paralysis due to inflammation of the peripheral nerves. Plasma exchange (PE), also known as plasmapheresis, has been studied as a treatment for GBS. This review, which updates previous analyses from 2001 and 2012, evaluates the efficacy and safety of plasma exchange in managing GBS. In one clinical trial involving 220 patients with severe GBS, the median time to regain the ability to walk with assistance was significantly shorter in the plasma exchange group (30 days) compared to the group receiving supportive care alone (44 days). Another trial with 91 patients who had mild GBS showed that the median time to the onset of motor recovery was shorter with plasma exchange (6 days) compared to supportive care (10 days). When data from three trials involving 349 patients were combined, moderate-quality evidence demonstrated that plasma exchange significantly increased the proportion of patients who regained the ability to walk with assistance after four weeks. The risk ratio (RR) for this outcome was 1.60, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.19 to 2.15. Additionally, in five trials with 623 participants, moderate-quality evidence showed that plasma exchange increased the likelihood of improving by at least one disability grade after four weeks (RR 1.64, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.96). Plasma exchange also reduced the time required to recover the ability to walk without assistance, as shown in three trials with 349 participants (RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.79). Furthermore, it decreased the need for artificial ventilation, as evidenced by five trials with 623 participants (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.74). However, there was a higher risk of relapse in the plasma exchange group compared to the control group by the end of follow-up. This finding was based on six trials with 649 participants, with a risk ratio of 2.89 (95% CI 1.05 to 7.93). Despite this, moderate-quality evidence indicated that after one year, patients treated with plasma exchange were more likely to achieve full recovery of muscle strength (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.45) and less likely to experience severe motor sequelae (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.96). Regarding mortality, high-quality evidence from six trials with 649 participants could neither confirm nor refute a reduction in the risk of death with plasma exchange compared to supportive care (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.65). Additionally, data from three trials involving 556 participants showed no significant increase in serious adverse events, such as infections, blood pressure instability, cardiac arrhythmias, or pulmonary embolism, in the plasma exchange group compared to the control group (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.13). In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence supports the use of plasma exchange in adults with Guillain-Barré syndrome, as it leads to significant improvements in recovery outcomes compared to supportive care alone. While there is a slightly increased risk of relapse within the first 6 to 12 months, plasma exchange is associated with better long-term recovery of muscle strength and a lower likelihood of severe residual weakness after one year. Importantly, plasma exchange does not appear to significantly increase the risk of serious adverse events.
